title: Spot the Big O — Real Problems
blurb: Actual solutions to classic LeetCode warm-ups. Read each one and name its worst-case TIME complexity. Watch for the same problem solved two different ways.

levels.title: L1 · Contains Duplicate (HashSet)
levels.hint: One pass over the array — and how fast is a HashSet add/lookup?

blocks.label: LeetCode 217 — Contains Duplicate

levels.explain: A single pass, and HashSet.Add / lookup are O(1) on average, so the whole method is O(n) — you trade O(n) space for the speed.

failStates.title: The hash set is the trick
failStates.explain: It's a single pass, and HashSet.Add / lookup are O(1) on average — so the whole thing is O(n). The O(n²) version is the brute-force double loop that compares every pair.

failStates.title: No sorting involved
failStates.explain: You'd get O(n log n) if you sorted first and scanned for neighbors. Here the hash set gives O(1) membership, so one pass = O(n).

levels.title: L2 · Two Sum (brute force)
levels.hint: Count the loops. What runs inside what?

blocks.label: LeetCode 1 — Two Sum, nested-loop version

levels.explain: Nested loops compare every pair of elements → O(n²). This is the version you’d want to improve in an interview.

failStates.title: Nested loops over the array
failStates.explain: For each i, the inner loop scans the rest of the array — n × n / 2 comparisons in the worst case → O(n²). This is the version you'd want to improve in an interview.

levels.title: L3 · Two Sum (hash map)
levels.prompt: Same problem, different approach. Time complexity?
levels.hint: The Dictionary replaces a search with a lookup. How fast is that lookup, and how many passes are left?

blocks.label: LeetCode 1 — Two Sum, dictionary version

levels.explain: The dictionary makes each “have I seen the complement?” check O(1), removing the inner loop — one pass = O(n), at the cost of O(n) extra space.

failStates.title: The dictionary removes the inner loop
failStates.explain: TryGetValue is O(1) on average, so the inner search vanishes — one pass = O(n). This is the exact 'nested loops → hash map' upgrade: O(n) time at the cost of O(n) extra space.

levels.title: L4 · Valid Anagram (sort)
levels.hint: There are two operations here — a comparison and a sort. Which one grows faster and dominates?

blocks.label: LeetCode 242 — Valid Anagram, sort version

levels.explain: SequenceEqual is O(n), but Array.Sort is O(n log n) and the largest term wins, so the method is O(n log n). Counting letters into a size-26 array instead of sorting would make it O(n).

failStates.title: The sort dominates
failStates.explain: SequenceEqual is O(n), but Array.Sort is O(n log n) — and the biggest term wins. So the whole method is O(n log n). (Counting letters into a size-26 array instead of sorting would make it O(n).)

failStates.title: Array.Sort isn't quadratic
failStates.explain: .NET's Array.Sort is O(n log n), not O(n²). There are no nested loops here.

levels.title: L5 · Valid Palindrome (two pointers)
levels.hint: Two pointers, sure — but how many characters do they cover between them?

blocks.label: LeetCode 125 — Valid Palindrome

levels.explain: The two pointers move toward each other and together cover all n characters once → O(n) time. Two pointers save space (O(1)), not time.

failStates.title: Two pointers still cross the whole string
failStates.explain: The two pointers move toward each other until they meet — together they cover all n characters → O(n) time. Two pointers cut the SPACE to O(1), but the time is still linear.

failStates.title: It's one pass, not nested
failStates.explain: There's a single while-loop; each character is looked at once. That's O(n).

levels.title: L6 · Majority Element
levels.hint: Is anything sorted here? How many passes over the array does it take?

blocks.label: LeetCode 169 — Majority Element, voting

levels.explain: It makes a single pass over the array, keeping just a running candidate and a counter (a trick called Boyer-Moore voting), so it's O(n) time and O(1) space — beating the sort-and-take-the-middle approach.

failStates.title: No sort — a single voting pass
failStates.explain: It's a single pass over the array (just a candidate and a counter — the Boyer-Moore voting trick), O(1) extra space → O(n) time. The alternative, sorting and taking the middle element, is O(n log n); this beats it.

levels.title: L7 · Single Number
levels.hint: It still runs one loop over the whole array — how many elements is that?

blocks.label: LeetCode 136 — Single Number

levels.explain: The loop runs once per element, so it's O(n) time. (The clever bit — XOR, the ^ operator that combines the numbers bit by bit — is what makes it O(1) space; it doesn't change the time.)

failStates.title: It still visits every element
failStates.explain: The loop still runs once per element → O(n) time. The clever, O(1)-space part is the single running total, not the time.

failStates.title: Single pass, no nesting
failStates.explain: One loop over the array, one operation each — O(n).

levels.title: L8 · Valid Parentheses (stack)
levels.hint: How many times is each character pushed or popped, and how fast are Push/Pop?

blocks.label: LeetCode 20 — Valid Parentheses

levels.explain: Each character is pushed or popped at most once, and both are O(1), so a single pass is O(n) time (with O(n) space for the stack).

failStates.title: Each char is pushed/popped once
failStates.explain: One pass over the string; Push and Pop are O(1) each, and every character is handled at most twice → O(n) time (and O(n) space for the stack).
